units.text: The building has the smell of old carpet and burnt coffee.
A radiator knocks somewhere behind the drywall.
Outside, the rain has been falling since morning without conviction.
Under the buzzing tube light, a waiting room of orange plastic chairs, and in them, a cardiac surgeon who used to hold hearts in his hands now holds a clipboard.

WENDELL PRUITT, 58, silver-haired, hands still gentle in the way of men who've been told for decades to be careful, sits across from the desk of OFFICER TANYA BELL, 40s, who has the tired patience of someone who has read every excuse ever invented.
Behind him his wife GLORIA, 50s, grips her purse.
At the counter, the clerk ODELL stamps forms, and the receptionist JUNO eats her lunch from a tupperware lid.
Dr Pruitt you understand the terms. No practising, no prescribing, no supervised access to patients. Not even a flu shot at the church.
units.name: BELL

units.text: I understand the terms Officer Bell. I'm not asking to practice. I'm asking to sit with one man. His name is Alvin Reese. He has eleven days. His family called me because no one else in this county would touch his valve.
units.name: WENDELL

units.text: No Gloria. Let me say it. Eleven years I've kept every rule they gave me. I didn't cut when the board told me not to cut. I didn't speak when the lawyers told me not to speak. A man is dying forty minutes from here and I know exactly how to stop it and I am sitting in a chair that's too small for me asking permission.
units.name: WENDELL

units.text: Bell closes the file very softly, the way you close a door on a sleeping child.
Mine, apparently. Doctor, I'm going to step out for ten minutes to take a phone call that I will not be able to remember in the morning. Odell. Juno. You didnt see him leave either.
units.name: BELL
